difficultyReason: Four-step chain with a biconditional hinge and modus tollens: All A are B; every B has C; C iff D; the specimen does not have D; therefore it cannot be A. Students must process a universal, a universal, a biconditional, and a negated particular before concluding with necessity. Traps preserve three of the four structural features while reversing one.
stimulus: Every case of bacterial meningitis involves inflammation of the meninges. Any patient with inflammation of the meninges exhibits elevated cerebrospinal protein. A patient exhibits elevated cerebrospinal protein if, and only if, a lumbar puncture yields a cloudy sample. The lumbar puncture performed on this patient yielded a clear sample. It follows that this patient cannot have bacterial meningitis.
questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most parallel to that in which one of the following?

choices.text: Every genuine Ming porcelain contains kaolin clay from Jingdezhen. Most objects containing kaolin clay from Jingdezhen show a distinctive thermoluminescence signature. An object shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature if, and only if, its firing temperature exceeded 1300 degrees Celsius. The disputed vase did not exceed 1300 degrees Celsius. So the disputed vase is probably not genuine Ming porcelain.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∀x(Ax → Bx); ∀x(Bx → Cx); ∀x(Cx ↔ Dx); ¬Dp; ∴ ¬Ap (with necessity). (A) replicates each step — two universals, a biconditional, a negated particular, and a necessity conclusion — simply reskinned in the porcelain domain.
explanations.B: Weakens the second premise from 'any/every' to 'most' and weakens the conclusion from necessity to probability — two quantifier/modal mismatches.
explanations.C: Only three premises, and the third step affirms the consequent rather than running modus tollens through a biconditional. Structurally reversed.
explanations.D: Replaces the biconditional with a one-way conditional ('only if') and softens the conclusion to 'may not' — both modal force and connective strength are off.
explanations.E: Two premises, not four; skips the inflammation and biconditional steps entirely.

difficultyReason: Four-step mixed-quantifier argument: some A are B; all B require C; C iff D; x is both A and B; therefore x probably requires D. The argument moves from existential to universal to biconditional and ends with a hedged conclusion that tracks the 'probably' licensed by instantiation from an existential base.
stimulus: Some medical studies that yield statistically significant results nevertheless have low replication rates. Every study with a low replication rate requires independent pre-registration to warrant continued funding. A study requires independent pre-registration if, and only if, its effect size falls below a conventional threshold. The Harmon study yielded statistically significant results and has a low replication rate. Therefore, the Harmon study's effect size probably falls below the conventional threshold.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A

An organization requires a restructuring plan if, and only if, its overhead ratio exceeds a conventional threshold. The Ardent Fund reports high donor retention and shows thin program margins. Therefore, the Ardent Fund's overhead ratio probably exceeds the conventional threshold.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most charitable organizations that report high donor retention show thin program margins. Every organization with thin program margins requires a restructuring plan. An organization requires a restructuring plan if, and only if, its overhead ratio exceeds a conventional threshold. The Ardent Fund reports high donor retention. Therefore, the Ardent Fund's overhead ratio exceeds the conventional threshold.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some charitable organizations that report high donor retention nevertheless show thin program margins. Every organization with thin program margins requires a restructuring plan. choices.label: E

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∃x(Ax ∧ Bx); ∀x(Bx → Cx); ∀x(Cx ↔ Dx); Ah ∧ Bh; ∴ probably Dh. (A) preserves all four elements: existential opener, universal middle, biconditional hinge, instantiation of both openers, hedged conclusion.
explanations.B: Converts the existential to 'most' and drops the hedge, then omits the second instantiation ('shows thin program margins'). Two shifts off parallel.
explanations.C: Weakens the second premise from 'every' to 'most' and the third from biconditional to one-way conditional.
explanations.D: Same premise set, but the conclusion reverses direction — it instantiates the consequent to derive the antecedent side, which is structurally a different move.
explanations.E: Opens with 'every' instead of 'some' and drops the hedge — conclusion shifts from probable to definite.

difficultyReason: Four-link contrapositive chain: A→B, B→C, C→D, ¬D, ∴ ¬A. Students must run modus tollens through three conditionals in succession. Traps shorten the chain, reverse a single step, or swap quantifier strength on one premise.
stimulus: If a currency union permits unlimited capital mobility, then its members must coordinate fiscal policy. If members must coordinate fiscal policy, then each member will need to cede some budgetary sovereignty. If each member cedes some budgetary sovereignty, then a central authority will have to ratify national budgets. No central authority has the power to ratify the member states' national budgets. Therefore, this currency union does not permit unlimited capital mobility.
questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A→B; B→C; C→D; ¬D; ∴ ¬A. (A) matches all four premises with the same conditional directions and ends with modus tollens through the full chain to deny the antecedent of the first premise.
explanations.B: Only three premises — the chain is shortened by one link, so the structure is three-step tollens, not four-step.
explanations.C: Replaces one premise with a 'most' quantifier and hedges the conclusion to 'probably' — two features off parallel.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent at the end — this is an invalid move, and the stimulus is valid, so the parallel fails.
explanations.E: Denies the antecedent to derive denial of the consequent — also invalid, and runs the chain in the reverse direction.

difficultyReason: Universal disjunctive plus a 'most' elimination plus instantiation, ending with a hedged positive conclusion. Four components: a universal conditional into a disjunction, a most-quantified negation of one disjunct, a particular instance, and a 'likely' conclusion on the surviving disjunct.
stimulus: Every contract that is unconscionable at the time of signing is either procedurally defective or substantively one-sided. Most contracts that are unconscionable at the time of signing are not procedurally defective. The Marsden agreement was unconscionable at the time of its signing. Therefore, the Marsden agreement is likely substantively one-sided.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

Most alloys that fracture under cyclic loading are not crystallographically flawed. The bracket from the Hargrove bridge fractured under cyclic loading. Therefore, the bracket is likely chemically contaminated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every alloy that fractures under cyclic loading is either crystallographically flawed or chemically contaminated. choices.label: C

choices.text: Every alloy that fractures under cyclic loading is either crystallographically flawed or chemically contaminated. explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∀x(Ax → (Bx ∨ Cx)); most A are ¬B; a is A; ∴ a is likely C. (A) matches each piece: a universal with a disjunctive consequent, a 'most' negation of one disjunct, an instantiation, and a hedged positive conclusion on the remaining disjunct.
explanations.B: Runs the 'most' in the opposite direction (most A are C, not most A are ¬B) and drops the hedge.
explanations.C: Softens the first premise from 'every' to 'most', weakening the universal backbone of the argument.
explanations.D: Replaces 'most' with 'no' — a universal negative rather than a hedged majority — and strengthens the conclusion from 'likely' to categorical.
explanations.E: Turns the disjunction into a conjunction, so the second premise (most aren't B) contradicts the first rather than narrowing it.

difficultyReason: Biconditional plus chain plus existential generalization: A ↔ B; B → C; some A are D; therefore some D are C. Students must combine a biconditional (treat as A → B), a conditional, and an existential subject to yield an existential conclusion — an inference type that hinges on carrying the existential through two universals.
stimulus: A wetland is classified as a vernal pool if, and only if, it dries completely for part of each year. Every wetland that dries completely for part of each year supports at least one obligate indicator species. Some vernal pools in the Redclay reserve also exhibit fairy-shrimp egg banks. Therefore, some wetlands in the Redclay reserve that exhibit fairy-shrimp egg banks support at least one obligate indicator species.
questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most parallel to that in which one of the following?

explanations.correct: Stimulus: Ax ↔ Bx; ∀x(Bx → Cx); ∃x(Ax ∧ Dx restricted to region R); ∴ ∃x(Dx ∧ Cx in R). (A) preserves the biconditional opener, the universal second step, the existential subject, and the existential conclusion at the same scope.
explanations.B: Downgrades the second premise from 'every' to 'most' and the conclusion from existential to 'most', changing two features.
explanations.C: Replaces the biconditional with a one-way 'only if' conditional — the biconditional strength is lost.
explanations.D: Strengthens both the existential premise and conclusion to universals ('every'), changing quantifier type.
explanations.E: Reverses the direction of the second premise, then draws a conclusion about being tonal rather than about the minimal-tone-pair property.

difficultyReason: Four-step argument mixing two universal conditionals, a 'most' generalization over the chain's endpoint, an instantiation, and a hedged conclusion. Students must recognize that the conclusion's 'probably' is licensed not by 'most' alone but by chaining two universals before meeting the 'most' premise.
stimulus: Any operating system that ships with the latest kernel patch supports hardware-level memory tagging. Every system that supports hardware-level memory tagging can run the new sandboxed runtime. Most systems that can run the new sandboxed runtime pass the FlexBench security audit. The server in our datacenter ships with the latest kernel patch. Therefore, the server in our datacenter will probably pass the FlexBench security audit.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∀x(Ax → Bx); ∀x(Bx → Cx); most Cx are Dx; Aa; ∴ probably Da. (A) mirrors all four steps: two universal conditionals forming a chain, a 'most' generalization over the chain endpoint, an instantiation of A, and a hedged conclusion of D.
explanations.B: Strengthens the third premise from 'most' to 'every' while keeping the conclusion hedged — the 'probably' no longer matches the now-universal chain.
explanations.C: Weakens the first premise from 'any' to 'most' and promotes the conclusion from 'probably' to categorical.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent at the end of the chain — concludes about the antecedent from the endpoint, reversing direction.
explanations.E: Reverses the direction of the third premise (most D are C, not most C are D) — cannot yield the same inference.

difficultyReason: Four-step argument combining a universal conditional, a contrapositive observation, and a disjunctive syllogism with a particular in one of the disjuncts. The contrapositive move eliminates one disjunct and forces the positive conclusion on the other.
stimulus: Every Indo-European language retains at least one trace of laryngeal consonants in its oldest strata. The language recorded on the Boglath tablets shows no trace of laryngeal consonants in any stratum. The Boglath language is either Indo-European or Pre-Hurrian. Therefore, the Boglath language is Pre-Hurrian.
questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∀x(Ax → Bx); ¬Ba; A∨C for a; ∴ C for a. (A) matches: a universal conditional, a negated particular consequent, a binary disjunction containing the class, and a positive conclusion on the alternative disjunct.
explanations.B: Weakens the first premise from 'every' to 'most' and hedges the conclusion to 'probably' — two structural features change.
explanations.C: Affirms the consequent and concludes on the wrong disjunct (Indo-European analog rather than the alternative) — reverses direction.
explanations.D: Only two premises, ending at the modus tollens negation; the disjunctive-syllogism step is missing entirely.
explanations.E: Uses the disjunction with an asserted disjunct as a premise rather than deriving it, and concludes about the consequent property, not the category.

difficultyReason: Four-step analogical argument with an embedded universal conditional and a hedged conclusion. Two cases share two properties; a universal links those properties to a third; one case has the third property; the conclusion transfers the property to the other case with 'likely'.
stimulus: The reform movements of eighteenth-century Denmark and eighteenth-century Tuscany shared two features: both were led by enlightened monarchs, and both enacted agrarian reforms before any constitutional reform. Every eighteenth-century reform movement that was led by an enlightened monarch and enacted agrarian reforms before constitutional reforms eventually produced a durable legal code. The Danish movement eventually produced a durable legal code. Therefore, the Tuscan movement likely produced a durable legal code as well.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

Every composition curriculum designed by a former novelist that sequenced revision before stylistic instruction eventually produced a signature student magazine. Rosedale's curriculum eventually produced a signature student magazine. Therefore, Finch's curriculum likely produced a signature student magazine as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The composition curricula of Rosedale Academy and Finch Academy shared two features. Rosedale's curriculum eventually produced a signature student magazine. Therefore, Finch's curriculum produced a signature student magazine.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: X and Y share properties P and Q; ∀z((Pz ∧ Qz) → Rz); X has R; ∴ Y likely has R. (A) mirrors the shared-property opener, the universal conditional over both properties, the single-case confirmation of R, and the hedged transfer to Y.
explanations.B: Drops the explicit naming of the two shared features and strips the hedge from the conclusion — two structural gaps.
explanations.C: Weakens the universal premise from 'every' to 'most' and promotes the conclusion from 'likely' to categorical.
explanations.D: Keeps all premises intact but adds an extra temporal claim ('before Finch's did') to the conclusion — an unlicensed addition.
explanations.E: Vague analogical premise ('several features') and no universal conditional — drops two of the four structural elements.

difficultyReason: Nested-conditional argument: if all A are B, then C; C is false; therefore some A are not B. Four structural elements to match — a conditional whose antecedent is itself a universal, a contrapositive application, the existential generalization licensed by the negation of a universal, and the explicit 'at least one' phrasing.
stimulus: If every eligible voter in Callenhurst registered by the deadline, then the preliminary turnout estimate would exceed 40,000. The preliminary turnout estimate does not exceed 40,000. Therefore, at least one eligible voter in Callenhurst did not register by the deadline.
questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most parallel to that in which one of the following?

The continuing-education log does not contain over 400 entries. Therefore, at least one licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge did not complete the refresher course.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If every licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course, then the continuing-education log would contain over 400 entries. The continuing-education log contains over 400 entries. Therefore, every licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course.

The continuing-education log does not contain over 400 entries. Therefore, most licensed pharmacists at Greerbridge did not complete the refresher course.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If every licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course, then the continuing-education log would contain over 400 entries. At least one licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge did not complete the refresher course. Therefore, the continuing-education log does not contain over 400 entries.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: (∀x Ax → Bx) → C; ¬C; ∴ ∃x(Ax ∧ ¬Bx). (A) replicates the nested conditional whose antecedent is a universal, runs modus tollens to deny the universal antecedent, and correctly draws the existential ('at least one ... did not') conclusion.
explanations.B: Affirms the consequent — concludes the universal from the numerical fact being true, an invalid move.
explanations.C: Replaces 'every' with 'most' in both antecedent and conclusion, so the negation of a 'most' claim is drawn instead of an existential.
explanations.D: Runs the conditional in the opposite direction: denies the universal to conclude the consequent's negation, reversing cause and effect.
explanations.E: Overshoots from 'at least one did not' to 'no one did' — a quantifier strength error at the conclusion.

difficultyReason: Four-step conjunctive-consequent plus biconditional structure: A → (B ∧ C); ¬B; B ↔ D; ∴ ¬A and ¬D. Students must derive two distinct negations — one by contrapositive of a conjunction and one through the biconditional — both with necessity.
stimulus: If a symphony is genuinely by Grazia, it has both a modulation to the flat mediant in its exposition and a triple-meter trio in its scherzo. The symphony on this score does not modulate to the flat mediant in its exposition. A symphony contains a modulation to the flat mediant in its exposition if, and only if, its autograph manuscript bears a triadic cipher in the margin. It follows that the symphony on this score is not genuinely by Grazia, and its autograph manuscript does not bear a triadic cipher in the margin.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

It follows that the coin in this collection is not a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, and its die does not have a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has either a quadriga on the obverse or a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection does not bear a quadriga. A coin bears a quadriga if, and only if, its die has a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position. It follows that the coin is not a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, and its die does not have a microscopic anchor mark.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has both a quadriga on the obverse and a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection does not bear a quadriga on the obverse. A coin bears a quadriga on the obverse only if its die has a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position. It follows that the coin is not a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, and its die probably lacks the anchor mark.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has both a quadriga on the obverse and a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection does not bear a facing Arethusa on the reverse. A coin bears a facing Arethusa if, and only if, its die has a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position. It follows that the coin bears a quadriga on the obverse, and its die does not have a microscopic anchor mark.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has both a quadriga on the obverse and a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection is not a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm. A coin bears a quadriga if, and only if, its die has a microscopic anchor mark. It follows that the coin does not bear a quadriga, and its die does not have the anchor mark.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A → (B ∧ C); ¬B; B ↔ D; ∴ ¬A ∧ ¬D. (A) preserves each step: a conditional with a conjunctive consequent, a negated conjunct, a biconditional binding that conjunct to a fourth property, and a two-part necessary conclusion negating both A and D.
explanations.B: Converts the conjunction in the consequent to a disjunction — denying one disjunct no longer licenses denying the conditional's antecedent on its own.
explanations.C: Replaces the biconditional with a one-way 'only if' conditional and softens one half of the conclusion to 'probably', breaking both connective strength and modal match.
explanations.D: Runs the negation on the wrong conjunct (Arethusa, not quadriga), then draws an unlicensed positive conclusion that the coin bears a quadriga — an inversion of the stimulus's moves.
explanations.E: Uses ¬A as a premise rather than deriving it, then draws ¬B as a conclusion — running the conditional in the wrong direction (denying the antecedent to derive a negated conjunct).
